description: Teammates at Johns Hopkins Applied Math
summary:
We, the Wizards of Math, built a Streamlit dashboard in Python 3 that analyzes long-term trends in nine NASA POWER variables (temperature, dew point, humidity, precipitation, wind, pressure and solar radiation) for Dallas, New York City and San Francisco from 1981 to today. For each city, it estimates the annual and seasonal rate of change per decade, with confidence intervals and Sen’s slope. It tests significance with a t-test and a Mann-Kendall test, both corrected for autocorrelation. It also tracks trends in extreme days and in day-to-day variability.

We also explore how predictable each variable is from day to day. Our model combines a linear trend, seasonal harmonics (1–4, adjustable) and an autoregressive model whose order is chosen by the Bayesian Information Criterion (up to 14 days) with an adjustable train-test split.

Whether you want to dig into decades of climate trends or see how far the past can predict the future (and what it can't), this dashboard has you covered. We encourage you to test and explore!
details:
This Streamlit dashboard, built in Python 3 on the NASA POWER daily API, tracks nine variables for San Francisco, New York, and Dallas: temperature (mean, high, low), dew point, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, surface pressure, and solar radiation (from 1984). Its long-term view shows each year’s value as a change from the 1991–2020 average. It estimates the trend per decade with least-squares and Sen’s slopes and marks a trend significant only when an autocorrelation-corrected t-test and Mann-Kendall test agree. The same analysis runs by season, for extreme days, and for day-to-day variability. Tests use yearly rather than daily values because daily data makes them overconfident: in simulations with no real trend, false alarms stayed at 5–9% with the correction but reached 25% without it.

The predictability view splits each day into three parts: seasonal cycle plus trend, persistence from recent days, and unpredictable surprise. The model is trained on earlier years and tested on later ones, and a horizon analysis shows how forecast skill fades from 1 to 30 days ahead. Units can be metric or US, and method details are in the GitHub repo.
